lead: An air-standard cycle replaces the burning of fuel by heat added from outside, and the exhaust by heat rejected, to a fixed mass of air treated as an ideal gas. It gives the highest efficiency an engine following that sequence of processes could reach, and lets us compare engine types on equal terms. The Otto cycle adds heat at constant volume (the SI engine), the Diesel cycle at constant pressure (the slow CI engine) and the dual cycle partly at each (the fast CI engine). Which cycle comes out best depends on what is held equal, and that comparison is the favourite long question of this chapter.
prereq: You need the compression ratio from engine terminology and components and the SI and CI processes from working principle of SI and CI engines.

items: The working fluid is a fixed mass of air, an ideal gas (pv = RT, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K), in a closed cycle.
Specific heats are constant: c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 and c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K, γ = c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub> = 1.4.
Combustion is replaced by heat added from a hot source, and the exhaust and intake by heat rejected at constant volume.
Compression and expansion are isentropic: no friction and no heat transfer to the walls.

blocks.text: The efficiency so found is called the air-standard efficiency. A real engine always reaches less; fuel-air cycles and actual cycle analysis explains how much less and why.

sections.h3: Otto cycle: heat at constant volume

items: 1→2 isentropic compression from v₁ to v₂ = v₁/r;
2→3 heat added at constant volume, q<sub>in</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₃ − T₂);
4→1 heat rejected at constant volume, q<sub>out</sub> = c<sub>v</sub>(T₄ − T₁).

blocks.text: With the pressure ratio α = p₃/p₂, the mean effective pressure is mep = p₁ r (r<sup>γ−1</sup> − 1)(α − 1)/[(γ − 1)(r − 1)]. Some syllabi call this the constant-volume cycle.
The Diesel cycle adds heat at constant pressure, 2→3, while the piston moves out; heat addition stops at the cut-off ratio ρ = v₃/v₂. Then qin = cp(T₃ − T₂) and

The bracket (ρ<sup>γ</sup> − 1)/[γ(ρ − 1)] is greater than 1 for every ρ > 1, so at the same r the Diesel cycle is less efficient than the Otto cycle, and it gets worse as the cut-off ratio grows (more fuel, more load).

The dual (limited-pressure) cycle adds heat first at constant volume, 2→3, with α = p₃/p₂, and then at constant pressure, 3→4, with the cut-off ratio ρ = v₄/v₃; expansion is 4→5 and rejection 5→1. Its efficiency is
Put ρ = 1 and it becomes the Otto formula; put α = 1 and it becomes the Diesel formula.

Draw the three cycles on a T-s diagram from the same state 1. Each adds heat q<sub>in</sub> and rejects heat q<sub>out</sub> along the same constant-volume line from v₁, and η = 1 − q<sub>out</sub>/q<sub>in</sub>. The cycle that rejects least heat for the same heat in is the most efficient.

head: Held equal
Efficiency order
Why
rows: Otto adds all its heat at the smallest volume, so it expands through the largest ratio and rejects least heat
the pressure limit lets the Diesel cycle use a much higher compression ratio
same reason; this is the limit set by the strength and the materials of the engine

blocks.text: The second and third rows are the fair comparison of real engines, because an engine is limited by the peak pressure its parts can carry, not by its compression ratio. That is why a CI engine, though it follows the “less efficient” cycle at equal r, is the more efficient engine. The two worked examples show it with numbers: the Diesel cycle at r = 16 reaches almost the same peak pressure as the Otto cycle at r = 8, and is about 5 points more efficient.

figure.caption: The two worked examples drawn to scale from 1 bar and 300 K. Both peak near 48 bar, and from v = 0.108 m³/kg they share almost the same expansion line, but the Diesel cycle compresses to half the volume first, so its loop (shaded) encloses 561 kJ/kg against the Otto cycle’s 450 kJ/kg.

spec.aria: Pressure against specific volume. A dashed Otto loop compresses from 0.861 to 0.108 cubic metres per kilogram, rises at constant volume to 48 bar and expands back. A shaded Diesel loop compresses to 0.054, adds heat at 48.5 bar to 0.108 and expands along nearly the same line.

examples.question: An Otto cycle has a compression ratio of 8. At the start of compression the air is at 1 bar and 300 K, and the maximum temperature is 1800 K. Take γ = 1.4, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718 kJ/kg·K and R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K. Find the pressure and temperature at each corner, the heat added, the net work, the efficiency and the mean effective pressure.
steps: State 3: constant volume, so p₃ = p₂ T₃/T₂ = 18.38 × 1800/689.2 = 48.0 bar.
Heat added: q<sub>in</sub> = 0.718 × (1800 − 689.2) = 797.5 kJ/kg. Heat rejected: q<sub>out</sub> = 0.718 × (783.5 − 300) = 347.1 kJ/kg.
examples.answer: p₂ = 18.4 bar, T₂ = 689 K; p₃ = 48.0 bar; T₄ = 784 K, p₄ = 2.61 bar; q<sub>in</sub> = 797.5 kJ/kg, w = 450.4 kJ/kg, η = 56.5 %, mep = 5.98 bar.

examples.question: A Diesel cycle has a compression ratio of 16 and a cut-off ratio of 2, starting from the same 1 bar and 300 K (c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K). Find the peak pressure, the corner temperatures, the efficiency and the mep, and compare with the Otto cycle of the first example.
steps: State 2: 16<sup>0.4</sup> = 3.031, so T₂ = 909.4 K; 16<sup>1.4</sup> = 48.50, so p₂ = p₃ = 48.5 bar. This is the peak pressure.

Comparison: peak pressures 48.5 and 48.0 bar, nearly equal, but the Diesel cycle gives 61.4 % against 56.5 % and more work per kg (561 against 450 kJ). At equal r = 16 an Otto cycle would give 67.0 %, so the order flips with what is held equal.
examples.answer: Peak pressure 48.5 bar; T₂ = 909 K, T₃ = 1819 K, T₄ = 792 K; η = 61.4 %, mep = 6.95 bar. At nearly the same peak pressure the Diesel cycle beats the Otto cycle by 4.9 points.

traps: Write the exponent: 8<sup>0.4</sup> = 2.297, not 8 × 0.4. Writing “80.4 = 2.297” loses the mark.
“Otto is more efficient than Diesel” is true only at the same compression ratio. At the same peak pressure the order reverses.
The cut-off ratio is v₃/v₂ in the Diesel cycle but v₄/v₃ in the dual cycle, because the dual cycle has an extra corner.
mep is net work divided by swept volume (v₁ − v₂), not by v₁; with kJ/kg and m³/kg the answer is in kPa.
Air-standard efficiency is not brake efficiency; it leaves out heat loss, friction and gas exchange.

quiz.a: Fixed mass of air as an ideal gas in a closed cycle; constant specific heats with γ = 1.4; heat added and rejected from outside instead of combustion and exhaust; isentropic compression and expansion.

quiz.q: Which cycle adds heat at constant volume, which at constant pressure, and which at both?
quiz.a: Otto at constant volume, Diesel at constant pressure, dual at both.

quiz.q: Why does the Otto efficiency depend only on r?
quiz.a: Both heat flows are c<sub>v</sub> times a temperature rise, and the isentropes give T₂/T₁ = T₃/T₄ = r<sup>γ−1</sup>, so q<sub>out</sub>/q<sub>in</sub> = 1/r<sup>γ−1</sup> whatever the heat added.

quiz.q: An Otto cycle has r = 10 and γ = 1.4. Find its efficiency.
A Diesel cycle has r = 16, ρ = 2 and γ = 1.4. Find its efficiency.
Rank the Otto, dual and Diesel cycles for the same r and heat input, and for the same peak pressure and heat input. Explain the reversal.
quiz.a: Same r: Otto > dual > Diesel, since Otto adds all its heat at the smallest volume. Same peak pressure: Diesel > dual > Otto, because the pressure limit lets the Diesel cycle run a much higher r, and it then rejects less heat.

quiz.q: Why does the Diesel efficiency fall as the load (cut-off ratio) rises?
quiz.a: More of the heat is added late, at larger volume, so it expands through a smaller ratio; the bracket (ρ<sup>γ</sup> − 1)/[γ(ρ − 1)] grows with ρ and η falls.

beyond: Engine simulation uses variable specific heats and real gas mixtures instead of a constant γ, and finite-time thermodynamics adds finite heat-transfer time to these cycles. The Atkinson and Miller cycles expand further than they compress; hybrid petrol engines use them. Search for Atkinson cycle, Miller cycle and finite-time Otto cycle.
